This paper focuses on the task of generating creative stories, which requires LMs to generate text: https://huggingface.co GoogleResearch/laion2B-highresolution14-dataset-mix.

To evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate both diverse and coherent language, we focus on the task of generating creative stories. 
\textbf{Story prompts} are commonly used to assess the creativity of LLMs, as they are more effective than other methods such as open-ended generation prompts, e.g., \texttt{Write a creative story} (Wang2024aicreativehumans}.

\section{Empirical Findings on Generating Diverse and Coherent Language}

\label{sec:findings}

We evaluate the ability of various LLMs to generate diverse and coherent language on two different tasks: (1) \emph{causality}, where the model needs to infer the causal relationship in the given language and (2) \emph{story generation}, where the model needs to generate creative and relevant stories. 

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

In the causality task, we assess the model's ability to reason about causal relationships and make correct inferences.
We use a set of 30 questions from the ALI benchmark \citep{gu2020looking}, which contains five questions for each of the following six sub-tasks: \emph{causal effects data} (\texttt{ce-d}), \emph{description reasons} (\texttt{dr}), \emph{description effects} (\texttt{de}), \emph{textual causal inference} (\texttt{ci}), \emph{common cause inference} (\texttt{ccai}), and \emph{necessary condition for effect} (\texttt{nec}).
We use the questions from the validation set of the ALI benchmark to evaluate the LMs' ability to infer causal relationships.
For each question, we provide the model with two sentences in a conversation format.
We then prompt the model with a question such as \emph{``What is the effect of the condition A?''} or \emph{``What is the necessary condition for the effect B?''}, where \emph{A} and \emph{B} are masks that are filled with names, places, etc.
We use the log-probability of the model to generate the next sentence, e.g., \emph{``B is raining in New York''}, as the score to determine whether the model makes a correct inference.
We average three runs of evaluations to reduce randomness.

In the story generation task, we evaluate the language models using three metrics: diversity, fluency, and relevance.
We use a set of 100 story prompts that were manually crafted for the 2024 Human Evaluation of AI Story Generation (HEAG 2024).
We divided the 100 story prompts into three categories based on their prompt length: \emph{basic (30--50)}, \emph{medium (50--80)}, and \emph{detailed (80--100)}.
The detailed prompt category is designed to provide more specific information about the story, while the basic category is designed to be more general and less detailed.
These prompts enable us to evaluate whether the ability of LLMs to generate more creative stories increases when more specific story information is provided. 
For each story prompt, we randomly sample 50 story completions from each model that we evaluate.
We use three automatic evaluation metrics to evaluate the quality of the generated stories: \emph{diversity}, \emph{fluency}, and \emph{relevance}.
We use an automatic metric that measures the \emph{diversity} of the generated stories.
We use a Gini coefficient \citep{parker2018towards}, which measures the average degree of inequality across different attributes.
In particular, we use the Gini coefficient metric (GC) across the story topics, genres, and writing styles of the generated stories. 
The \emph{fluency} metric measures how well the generated story fits the story prompt provided to the model. 
To measure the fluency of the generated story, we use ROUGE \citep{lin-2004-rouge} to compare the generated story to the reference articles, and we report the ROUGE-1 (ER) metric.
The \emph{relevance} metric measures the degree to which the generated story is aligned with the specified story prompt. 
To measure the relevance of the generated story, we use the ROUGE-1 (ER) metric that compares the generated story to the story prompt provided to the model.
We then average the ROUGE-1 (ER) metric across the prompts within a similar category and report the average relevance score.
We use three different categories of prompts: \emph{basic topic-based story prompts}, \emph{medium topic-based story prompts}, and \emph{detailed topic-based story prompts}.
We average three runs of evaluation to reduce randomness.

\subsection{Key Experimental Findings}

\textbf{Diversity and Coherence.}
Table~\ref{tab:eval_results} summarizes the evaluation results for various language models on the causality and story benchmarks.
Among all evaluated models, GPT-4 achieves the highest accuracy on the causality tasks, which indicates its superior ability to infer causal relationships and make correct judgments. 
GPT-J-train, a model trained on the LAION 2B High Resolution dataset following \cite{yuan24gptj}, has the highest diversity score across all evaluated story prompts, indicating its ability to generate diverse language. 
It is also noteworthy that GPT-4 has the lowest diversity but the highest performance on the causality tasks, suggesting its ability to adapt to specific instructions and generate more focused content. 
We also observe that larger models do not necessarily generate more diverse stories. 
For example, the diversity scores of Llama 2 7B and 70B are similar across all categories of story prompts, suggesting that the ability of models to generate diverse language does not necessarily increase with their parameter sizes. 
We also find that GPT-J-train and GPT-4 achieve the highest performance on some relevant metrics, indicating their ability to generate language that is both diverse and relevant to the given story prompts.

\textbf{Creativity and Comprehension.}
Figure~\ref{fig:diversity_compare} illustrates how the diversity of the generated stories increases as the input prompt length increases. 
This demonstrates that the ability of language models to generate more creative language increases when more specific information about the story is provided in the story prompts. 
Interestingly, we observe that the LMs trained on Laion2B, such as GPT-J-train, can generate more diverse stories than closed-source LMs, such as GPT-4 and Llama 3 8B, when given short prompts.
This suggests that the ability of LMs to generate diverse stories might not be well-aligned with their training data (\emph{generic}). 
When specific story prompts are provided, the performance of LMs increases significantly, indicating their ability to generate more creative stories when the given information is well-aligned with their training data.

\textbf{Causality.}
Figure~\ref{fig:scale} demonstrates how the performance of language models on various tasks increases with the increasing number of model parameters and training data. 
Specifically, for the causality tasks, the accuracy scores improve with the increasing number of training data, suggesting that the ability of LMs to infer causal relationships might be affected by the amount of training data.
It is also noteworthy that larger models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tend to have a slower improvement rate in accuracy and fluency scores. 
We hypothesize that this might be due to the difficulty of inferring causal relationships.

\textbf{Imagination.}
To evaluate the ability of LMs to generate language that diverges significantly from their training data, 
we use 30 story prompts that are intentionally designed to be out-of-distribution (OOD) to the training data.
We find that the diversity and relevance scores of the stories generated by GPT-J-train, which was trained on the Laion2B dataset, are only slightly lower than those of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, which were not trained on that dataset at all. 
This evaluation approach enables us to determine whether the LMs can generate creative and relevant text when the prompts are well-aligned with their training data.
If the generated text is highly related to the dataset used for training, we might not be able to evaluate the imagination of the LMs.

\textbf{Trade-offs.}
Figure~\ref{fig:scale} demonstrates how the diversity, fluency, and relevance of the generated text tradeoff as the models increase in size and training data. 
Specifically, for the causality tasks, the accuracy scores improve with the increasing number of training data, suggesting that the ability of LMs to infer causal relationships might be affected by the amount of training data. 
It is also noteworthy that larger models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tend to have a slower improvement rate in accuracy and fluency scores. 
We hypothesize that this might be due to the difficulty of inferring causal relationships.

\textbf{Human Evaluation.}
\label{sec:human_evaluation}
We use human evaluation to assess the quality of the generated stories. 
This approach complements automatic evaluation methods by incorporating human judgments and preferences. 
We randomly sample 50 generated stories for each evaluated model and ask 10 raters to evaluate the sampled stories. 
We use a 10-point Likert scale to score each story and use ``2'' as the lowest score and ``5'' as the highest.
We average the ratings across all samples and raters as the human average (``Avg. H'' in Tables~\ref{tab:eval_results} and~\ref{tab:eval_results_lower}).
Results in these tables suggest that human-written stories got a score of 3.855, which is higher than that of GPT-4 and similar to that of GPT-J-train. 
This finding implies that closed-source LMs such as GPT-4 might still be far less ``talented'' than commonly perceived by humans.
Among all evaluated models, GPT-4 performs best on human evaluation and causality tasks and GPT-J-train is the best-performing model on the story generation task. 


\section{Related Works}

\label{sec:related_works}

\textbf{Training Data Leakage.}
We are aware that some language models, such as GPT-4, have been trained to predict the next token in text corpora~\citep{gpt4}.
This might lead to data leakage in our story evaluation if the training data contains stories similar to ours. 
However, we argue that such training approach is orthogonal to our evaluation and even complementary.
Even if the training data contains \emph{the same story} used for evaluation, it does not necessarily mean that the language model can generate \emph{that same story}.
Our evaluation measures the ability of LMs to generate diverse and coherent language in a specific scenario.
If a language model trained on the same story generated \emph{that same story} across multiple runs, it would indicate that it failed our evaluation. 
If we want a language model that generates \emph{the same story} across all runs, we should evaluate it on its adherence to instructions, not its ability to generate diverse and coherent language.
\textbf{Creative Language.}
Creativity is an important task for LLMs because it allows humans to interact with LMs in more natural ways and achieve greater efficiency in completing complex tasks together~\citep{socher2023enhancing, bansal2023composing, bansal2024intelligent}.
To evaluate the creativity of LLMs, many human evaluations and automatic evaluation methods have been proposed to assess their ability to generate language that is novel, diverse, and coherent~\citep{chakrabarty24artifice, wang24noise, Goyle2024HarnessingHP, Zhang2025NoveltyBenchEN, zhong2024lot, cheng24automated, Goyle24cow, Chow2024InferenceAwareFF}.
We implement the \emph{basic}, \emph{medium}, and \emph{detailed topic-based story prompts}, which are designed to evaluate the comprehension ability of LLMs by providing more specific information about the story. 
In addition to the story prompts used for evaluation, we also evaluate the language models using ChatGPT to assess their ability to generate diverse and coherent language.
We use a specific instruction to prompt the model, which is as follows: 
\emph{Generate a creative and diverse story for me.}
Previous studies have shown that providing specific instructions can improve the performance of language models on various tasks~\citep{wei22cot, monea23pass, mrc21lai, cobbe21efficiency, mishra23selfrefine}.
\textbf{Model Scaling.}
The ability of LMs to generate diverse and coherent language is crucial for their practical applications, such as writing, creating jokes, and generating scientific hypotheses~\citep{denovo23watson, rives21genome, kitouni24factorization,  nguyen24sequence, deepseekAI2024, lu2024evolution, nguyen24sequence, hasan2024evolution}.
Previous studies have demonstrated that the performance of LMs on some language understanding tasks improves as the number of parameters and training data increase~\citep{kale2024scaling, Muennighoff25s1, Wu2024InferenceSL}.
However, other studies have shown that some abilities of LMs, such as mathematical creativity and comprehension, do not necessarily improve with increasing scale and training data~\citep{lee24arithmetic, bansal25haramours, Snell2024ScalingLT}.
Our findings also suggest that the scalability of LMs on causality and story generation tasks varies significantly. 
For the causality task, the accuracy scores improve with the increasing number of training data, suggesting that the ability of LMs to infer causal relationships might be affected by the amount of training data. 
On the other hand, the accuracy and fluency scores tend to plateau for the story generation task as the models increase in size and training data. 
This suggests that the ability of LMs to generate diverse and coherent language might not necessarily improve with increasing scale and training data. 


\section{Limitations and Future Works}

We use instruction prompting to generate stories. 
Previous studies have shown that instruction prompting is an effective way to assess the language comprehension ability of LLMs~\citep{wei22cot, monea23pass, mrc21lai, cobbe21efficiency, mishra23selfrefine}.
We use instructions that provide more specific information about the story to evaluate the comprehension ability of LLMs.
In the future, we plan to expand the evaluation dataset to include different domains and domains to evaluate the language models on diverse and consistent language. 
We also plan to investigate the ability of language models to generate creative and coherent language in different domains and domains.
We will also explore the ability of LLMs to generate diverse and consistent language in different domains and domains. 
We will conduct additional human evaluations to better assess the quality of the generated stories. 


\section{Conclusions}

We study the ability of LLMs to generate diverse and coherent language in this paper.
Specifically, we evaluate the language models on causality and story generation tasks to assess their ability to generate language that is novel, diverse, and coherent.
Among all evaluated models, GPT-4 Turbo Model and GPT-J-train perform best on causality and story generation tasks, respectively, and GPT-4 performs best on human evaluation. 
However, we observe that closed-source LMs might still be far less ``talented'' than commonly perceived by humans.
We also find that the performance of LMs on the story generation task does not necessarily improve with increasing scale and training data. 
We hope that our findings can inspire future research to improve the ability of LMs to generate diverse and consistent language.
